office.h1: Social Security Offices in the Bronx, NY
office.title: Social Security Office in the Bronx, NY: Locations & Services (2026)
office.meta: Complete guide to Social Security Administration offices in the Bronx, NY. Addresses, phone, hours, services, and how to choose the right office for your address.
office.intro: The Bronx has multiple Social Security Administration offices serving its 1.4 million residents across distinct neighborhoods. Unlike most U.S. cities with one main SSA office, the Bronx has five locations specifically because of population density and demographic need. This page gathers everything you need: which office serves your area, services available, hours, appointments, and tips to make the trip efficient.

sections.heading: The quick answer
sections.body: The Bronx is served by five Social Security Administration offices: Concourse Village West (the largest), South Bronx (East 149th St), Tremont (East Tremont Ave), Fordham (Webster Ave), and Wakefield (White Plains Rd). Each office handles all SSA services. The office you should visit depends on your home address. Call 1-800-772-1213 or use ssa.gov/locator to confirm the right one.

sections.heading: The five Social Security offices in the Bronx
body: 820 Concourse Village West, Bronx, NY 10451 — The largest and most centrally located office, near Yankee Stadium. Serves Concourse, Mott Haven, Highbridge, and the South-central Bronx. Accessible from the B, D, and 4 trains at Yankee Stadium-161st Street.
820 East 149th St, Bronx, NY 10455 — The South Bronx office serves Mott Haven, Melrose, Hunts Point, and Port Morris. Closest subway is 3rd Avenue-149th Street on the 2 and 5 lines.
1611 East Tremont Ave, Bronx, NY 10460 — Serves Tremont, Belmont, West Farms, Crotona, and Morris Park. Closest subway is West Farms Square-East Tremont on the 2 and 5 lines.

2702 Webster Ave, Bronx, NY 10458 — The Fordham office serves Fordham, University Heights, Kingsbridge Heights, and Bedford Park. Closest subway is Fordham Road on the B and D lines, or the Metro-North Fordham station.
4775 White Plains Rd, Bronx, NY 10470 — Serves Wakefield, Williamsbridge, Eastchester, and the northern Bronx neighborhoods.

sections.heading: Which office should you visit
body: The SSA assigns each address to a specific field office based on ZIP code. You generally must visit the office that serves your address, though for most services any office can help. To confirm which office serves your specific address, use the official SSA office locator at ssa.gov/locator with your ZIP code.
If you cannot easily get to your assigned office, call 1-800-772-1213 and ask. Most services can be handled at any Bronx office, and many do not require an in-person visit at all.

sections.heading: What you can do at any Bronx SSA office
body: Every Bronx office handles the full range of SSA services: apply for a first-time Social Security card, replace a lost card, change a name on the card, apply for disability benefits (SSDI and SSI), apply for retirement, apply for Medicare, get a Social Security number for a newborn, and many other services.

For routine services the SSA now handles online — replacement cards if you qualify, retirement applications, address changes, benefit verification letters — you may not need to visit any office at all. The ssa.gov website is the SSA's first-choice channel for most simple transactions.

sections.heading: Key information for all Bronx offices
items: National SSA phone line: 1-800-772-1213 (handles all offices).
Hours: generally Monday-Friday business hours (Wednesdays often close earlier).
Closed: weekends and federal holidays.
Walk-ins accepted, but appointments significantly reduce wait time.
Bilingual service (English/Spanish) at all Bronx offices.
Bring ORIGINAL documents only — no photocopies.

items.q: Can I visit any Bronx SSA office, or only the one for my ZIP code?
items.a: For most services, you can visit any office. For some complex local matters, your assigned office may need to handle it. When in doubt, call 1-800-772-1213 first.

items.q: Which Bronx office has the shortest wait time?
items.a: This varies day to day. Generally, mid-week mornings have shorter waits than Mondays or days following holidays. Appointments at any office reduce wait time significantly compared to walk-ins.

items.q: Are all Bronx SSA offices wheelchair accessible?
items.a: Yes. All SSA field offices, including all Bronx locations, must meet federal accessibility standards. Mobility assistance is available — request it when booking your appointment if needed.

items.q: What is the easiest office to reach by subway?
items.a: Concourse Village West at 820 Concourse Village West is right by the Yankee Stadium-161st Street station, served by the B, D, and 4 lines — among the most-connected in the borough.

office.h1: Social Security Office Hours in the Bronx
office.title: SSA Office Hours in the Bronx, NY (2026 Schedule)
office.meta: Current Social Security office hours for all five Bronx offices. Days open, federal holiday closures, and Wednesday early-close schedule for 2026.
office.intro: Knowing the Social Security office hours in the Bronx saves a wasted trip across the borough. The SSA's schedule has a few quirks — including Wednesday early closes and a long list of federal holiday closures — that catch many people out. This page explains the current hours for all five Bronx offices, the federal holidays when they close, and how to confirm hours before visiting.

sections.heading: The quick answer
sections.body: All five Bronx SSA offices are generally open Monday through Friday during standard business hours, with Wednesdays often closing earlier (around noon) for staff casework time. All offices are closed on weekends and every federal holiday. Hours can change without notice, so confirm by calling 1-800-772-1213 before any visit.

sections.heading: The Wednesday early-close
body: Most SSA field offices nationwide — including all Bronx offices — close earlier on Wednesdays, typically around noon. This is to give staff time to process the casework backlog without the pressure of walk-in visits. A Wednesday afternoon visit will almost always find the office closed.
If you need afternoon service, plan for Monday, Tuesday, Thursday, or Friday. Mornings are universally busier than afternoons, so a Tuesday or Thursday afternoon generally has the shortest wait time.

sections.heading: Federal holidays when all Bronx offices are closed
items: New Year's Day (January 1).
Martin Luther King Jr. Day (third Monday in January).
Presidents Day (third Monday in February).
Memorial Day (last Monday in May).
Juneteenth National Independence Day (June 19).
Independence Day (July 4).
Labor Day (first Monday in September).
Columbus Day (second Monday in October).
Veterans Day (November 11).
Thanksgiving Day (fourth Thursday in November).
Christmas Day (December 25).

sections.heading: How to use the hours efficiently
body: Best practice: schedule an appointment in advance by calling 1-800-772-1213. With an appointment you will be seen close to your scheduled time even on busy days. Walk-ins are accepted but mean 1-2 hour waits at peak times.

For quick services (updating an address, requesting a benefit verification letter), check first whether the request can be completed online at ssa.gov — many of these no longer require an office visit at all, eliminating the hours question entirely.

items.q: Are any Bronx SSA offices open on weekends?
items.a: No. All SSA field offices, including every Bronx location, are closed on Saturdays and Sundays. Use ssa.gov for any service available online.

items.q: What if I arrive close to closing time?
items.a: You may be turned away if there is not enough time to process your visit. Plan to arrive at least 30 minutes before closing — and earlier on Wednesdays when offices close around noon.

items.q: Can I call my Bronx office directly to confirm hours?
items.a: Direct local phone lines for field offices have been replaced by the national line at 1-800-772-1213. That number can confirm current hours for any specific Bronx office.

items.q: Are hours different around holidays?
items.a: Yes. Around major holidays, offices may have modified hours in addition to the holiday closure itself. Always confirm before visiting during holiday weeks.

office.h1: How to Book an Appointment at a Bronx SSA Office
office.title: Book a Social Security Appointment in the Bronx, NY (2026)
office.meta: How to schedule an appointment at any Bronx Social Security office. Why appointments save hours of waiting, and what documents to bring.
office.intro: Walking into a Bronx SSA office without an appointment can mean waiting 1-2 hours during busy periods. With an appointment, the same visit typically takes 15-30 minutes total. This page explains how to schedule one, why it makes such a difference in the Bronx specifically, and what to be ready to say when you call.

sections.heading: The quick answer
sections.body: To book an appointment at any Bronx SSA office, call the national SSA line at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY: 1-800-325-0778) Monday through Friday during business hours. Tell the representative you want an appointment at a specific Bronx office and what service you need. Appointments are usually available within 2-4 weeks. There is no online appointment booking for general services at the time of writing.

sections.heading: Why an appointment matters in the Bronx
body: Bronx SSA offices serve one of the densest, most demand-heavy populations of any borough. Walk-in waits of 1-2 hours are routine at peak times. With an appointment, you are typically seen within 5-15 minutes of your scheduled slot, and the visit itself takes 15-30 minutes.

Beyond time savings, an appointment also lets you know exactly what documents to bring — the representative who books your slot will tell you precisely what is needed for your specific service. That eliminates the most common cause of wasted trips: arriving without the right documents.

sections.heading: How to book step by step

items.a: This is the national SSA line and the only way to book an appointment at a Bronx field office. Have a pen ready to write down the appointment time and the required documents.

items.q: Step 2 - Specify the Bronx office
items.a: State clearly which Bronx office you want (Concourse Village, South Bronx, Tremont, Fordham, or Wakefield) and what service you need. The representative will check availability across nearby offices if needed.

items.q: Step 3 - Confirm what to bring
items.a: Once your appointment is confirmed, the representative will list exactly which documents are required. Write everything down — bringing the wrong documents wastes the trip.

items.q: Step 4 - Arrive 15 minutes early
items.a: On the day, arrive at the office at least 15 minutes before your slot to allow for security screening and check-in.

sections.heading: What to do if you cannot get an appointment soon enough
body: If the wait for an appointment is too long for your situation, consider whether your need can be handled online or by phone. Many SSA services do not require an in-person visit at all: retirement applications, replacement card requests, benefit verifications, address changes, and direct deposit updates can be done at ssa.gov.
If you genuinely need an in-person visit and cannot wait, walk-ins are accepted. Try to arrive at opening on a non-Monday, non-Wednesday morning for the shortest typical wait.

items.q: Can I book online?
items.a: At the time of writing, the SSA does not offer online appointment booking for most general services. Appointments are scheduled by calling 1-800-772-1213.

items.q: How far in advance should I call?
items.a: 2-4 weeks is typical, but availability varies by office and season. Call as soon as you know you need an appointment, especially during tax season or year-end.

items.q: What if I miss my appointment?
items.a: Call 1-800-772-1213 to reschedule. Missing without rescheduling can mean a longer wait for the next available slot.

items.q: Can I request bilingual service?
items.a: Yes. When you book, tell the representative you need a Spanish-speaking representative. All Bronx offices provide bilingual service given the borough's demographics.

items.q: Is there parking at any office?
items.a: Limited street parking is available near most offices, with time restrictions. The Concourse Village West and Wakefield offices have somewhat more parking availability than the central Bronx offices, but public transit is still strongly recommended.

office.h1: What Documents to Bring to a Bronx SSA Office
office.title: SSA Required Documents Checklist for Bronx Offices (2026)
office.meta: Complete checklist of what to bring to a Bronx Social Security office visit. Originals only, common mistakes, and what each service requires in 2026.
office.intro: The most common reason a trip to a Bronx SSA office is wasted is bringing the wrong documents — or photocopies instead of originals. This guide breaks down exactly what to bring for each common service, the rules that catch people out, and the gotchas specific to New York State documentation.

sections.heading: The quick answer
sections.body: The SSA requires ORIGINAL documents — not photocopies — for almost every service. They will photocopy them on the spot and hand the originals back. The exact documents depend on the service: SSN applications need proof of citizenship/status and identity; name changes need legal name-change documents; disability requires medical records; retirement needs birth certificate and proof of citizenship. When in doubt, bring more than you think you need.

sections.heading: The cardinal rules
body: Rule 1: ORIGINALS ONLY. The SSA does not accept photocopies for almost any document. They will photocopy your originals while you wait and return them in the same visit. Do not mail originals unless explicitly instructed.
Rule 2: UNEXPIRED. IDs and passports must be current, not expired. Birth certificates are an exception — they do not expire and originals are fine.

Rule 3: CERTIFIED, NOT NOTARIZED. For birth certificates, divorce decrees, and similar documents, you need a CERTIFIED copy with the official seal of the issuing agency — not a notarized photocopy. In New York, certified birth certificates come from the New York State Department of Health or the NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene.

items.q: First-time Social Security card
items.a: Form SS-5, original birth certificate (for U.S. citizens) or current immigration documents (for non-citizens), and original photo ID. For minors, parent's ID is required.

items.q: Replacement card
items.a: Form SS-5 and original unexpired photo ID (NYS driver's license, NYS ID, or U.S. passport). If your name has changed since the last card, also bring the legal name-change document.

items.q: Name change
items.a: Form SS-5, original legal name-change document (marriage certificate, divorce decree with name change, court order), and original photo ID — ideally in the new name already.

items.q: Apply for retirement
items.a: Birth certificate, proof of U.S. citizenship/lawful status, last year's W-2 or tax return, military discharge papers if pre-1968 service, and bank info for direct deposit.

items.q: Apply for disability
items.a: Medical records and provider list, medications list, work history (15 years), recent W-2, birth certificate, and bank info for direct deposit. SSI applications need detailed financial records in addition.

items.q: Apply for Medicare (without already on Social Security)
items.a: Birth certificate, proof of U.S. citizenship, and proof of any prior creditable coverage if delaying parts.

sections.heading: Common mistakes in the Bronx
body: Bringing photocopies instead of originals. This is the number-one wasted trip across every Bronx office.
Expired IDs. A NYS driver's license that expired last month will be rejected. Renew at a DMV first, then visit SSA.
Notarized copies instead of certified copies. A notary stamp on a photocopy is not the same as a certified document from the issuing agency.
Forgetting Form SS-5 for SSN-related services. You can complete it at the office, but pre-filling at home saves time.
Not bringing supporting documents 'just in case.' If a service might need extra documentation, bring it. Going home to retrieve something is far worse than carrying an extra envelope.

items.q: Will the SSA accept a digital copy on my phone?
items.a: Generally no. Original physical documents are required. Some limited exceptions exist for specific situations — ask when you book your appointment.

items.q: What if my documents are in another language?
items.a: Foreign documents must be accompanied by a certified English translation. Bronx offices have Spanish-language support but written documents in other languages still need certified translations.

items.q: How do I get a certified New York birth certificate?
items.a: For births in New York City: NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (vital records). For births elsewhere in New York State: the New York State Department of Health. Certified copies cost a small fee and arrive by mail in a few days to weeks.

items.q: Can someone else bring my documents for me?
items.a: For most services, no. You must appear in person with your own documents. The SSA does not accept third-party representatives without specific legal authority such as a Power of Attorney for certain situations.

office.h1: Social Security Services in Spanish in the Bronx
office.title: SSA Spanish-Language Services in the Bronx, NY (2026)
office.meta: Bilingual Spanish/English Social Security services in the Bronx. Spanish-speaking representatives, translated forms, and call line at 1-800-772-1213.
office.intro: Spanish is a primary language for a significant portion of Bronx residents, and the Social Security Administration offers full Spanish-language service at every Bronx office. This page explains how to access Spanish-speaking representatives, request bilingual support, and find SSA materials in Spanish. Knowing how to navigate Social Security in Spanish from the Bronx is essential for many borough residents.

sections.heading: The quick answer
sections.body: Every Bronx SSA office provides full bilingual service in English and Spanish. The national SSA phone line at 1-800-772-1213 also offers Spanish service — press the option for Español when prompted. Forms, brochures, and the SSA website are all available in Spanish at ssa.gov/espanol. When scheduling an appointment, request a Spanish-speaking representative.

sections.heading: How to request a Spanish-speaking representative
body: When calling 1-800-772-1213, the system prompts in English first but follows with the Spanish option. Press or say the Spanish option to be routed to a bilingual representative. The phone line offers full Spanish service for any question or request that can be handled by phone.

When scheduling an appointment at any Bronx office, request a Spanish-speaking representative explicitly: 'I need an appointment with a Spanish-speaking representative.' This ensures bilingual support during your visit. Walk-ins requesting Spanish service may experience longer waits than English-only walk-ins, depending on the day.

sections.heading: SSA Spanish website and materials
body: The SSA maintains a full Spanish-language website at ssa.gov/espanol with all the major services translated: applying for benefits, replacing cards, requesting verification letters, understanding eligibility. Forms commonly used in the Bronx — Form SS-5 (SSN card application), benefit verification, address change — are available in Spanish from the SSA.
Educational materials on programs like SSDI, SSI, and Medicare are also available in Spanish, including printed brochures distributed at Bronx offices and downloadable PDFs from ssa.gov/espanol.

sections.heading: Spanish-language services at Bronx offices
items: Bilingual representatives available at all five Bronx SSA offices.
Spanish phone service via 1-800-772-1213.
Forms in Spanish, including SS-5 (card application).
Brochures and educational materials in Spanish at all offices.
Bilingual signage at most office entrances.
Online services at ssa.gov/espanol for those who prefer digital.

sections.heading: If your primary language is neither English nor Spanish
body: The SSA offers free interpreter services in dozens of languages by phone. When you call 1-800-772-1213 or visit a Bronx office, request an interpreter for your language. Interpreter services are free and confidential. Common languages with interpreter availability include Bengali, Chinese (Mandarin and Cantonese), French, Arabic, Russian, Albanian, and many others — all relevant for the diverse population of the Bronx.

Written documents in languages other than English or Spanish still require a certified English translation when submitted to the SSA. Verbal interpretation during the appointment is free; written translations of your supporting documents are your responsibility.

items.q: Are SSA Spanish-language services the same quality as English?
items.a: Yes. Bilingual representatives are trained on the same procedures and have access to the same information. Documents submitted in Spanish are handled with the same processing time as English.

items.q: Can I bring a family member or friend to translate?
items.a: You can bring someone to support you, but the SSA prefers to use official interpreter services for accuracy in benefit-related conversations. Family members may translate but the SSA may verify key details directly through their interpreter service.

items.q: Are all SSA forms available in Spanish?
items.a: Most major forms are, including Form SS-5 for card applications. Less common forms may only be in English, but Spanish-speaking representatives can help complete them.

items.q: Can I do everything in Spanish at ssa.gov?
items.a: Yes — ssa.gov/espanol mirrors the main site in Spanish for major services. Some less-used pages may still be English-only, but all primary applications and account services are available in Spanish.
